articles.title: Homeowners continue cleanup after EF-1 tornado ravages neighborhoods in Northwest Indiana
articles.description:
Laura Ramos said she grabbed her cat and hunkered down in her bathtub Tuesday after her phone sounded an alarm warning that a tornado was headed her way.

Moments later, a tornado with wind gusts of 86 to 110 mph tore through her Munster, Indiana, neighborhood, knocking down power lines, uprooting trees and buckling sidewalks. The National Weather Service confirmed the EF-1 tornado touched down on the north side of town.

“It’s true what they say that it sounds like a train going over your roof,” said Ramos, 59.

Indiana Gov. Mike Braun declared a state of emergency Thursday in response to widespread damage in Northwest Indiana from this week’s severe storms that brought flooding and tornadoes to the state. Weather officials also confirmed an EF-2 tornado touched down in St. John, Indiana.

“Hoosiers’ safety is my top priority,” Braun said in a statement. “Our state response is fully mobilized, resources are moving where they’re needed, and we will continue working around the clock to support every impacted community.”

Braun also deployed the Indiana National Guard to help communities in Lake County clear tree debris, according to the Lake County Homeland Security and Emergency Management Agency.

Ramos' home was damaged when the tornado knocked down two of her trees, causing one to land on her house. On Thursday morning, her sister-in-law and brother-in-law drove in from Chicago to help her with the cleanup.

After the tornado passed, Ramos said she was overcome with emotion as she surveyed the damage to her neighborhood. She moved into her home in the 8400 block of Moraine Avenue in 2009 and said she barely recognized the area after the storm.

“I made the mistake of going on a walk around the block, and I broke down and cried because everybody’s front yards were flipped over,” she said.

Though she suffered damage to her roof, Ramos said it could have been much worse.

On Thursday afternoon, several of Ramos’ neighbors were seen sawing through fallen trees and raking up leaves and debris. The steady hum of generators could also be heard as residents worked to keep their homes powered.

Ramos said she only had a small generator with enough power to charge her cellphone.

Thousands remained without power Thursday after the severe storms knocked out service for a majority of customers.

NIPSCO said late Thursday morning it had restored service for 75,000 of the 313,000 electric customers who lost service. The utility service said it was the largest outage event in its history.

It was unclear how long it would take to restore power. Many residents in Munster and Hammond said they were prepared to remain without electricity through at least the weekend, while some expected the outages to last even longer.

At a Hammond gas station, cars lined up Thursday to fill gas cans to fuel generators keeping homes powered after the storm.

Gil Mellendorf, of Munster, stopped at the BP at 6906 Hohman Ave. to get gas for the generators at his home. The gas station was also running on generators.

Mellendorf said his street flooded during Tuesday’s storm, and his biggest concern was keeping the sump pump running to prevent his home from flooding.

“It’s a lot going on right now,” said Mellendorf, 67. “But we’re veterans when it comes to storms.”

Mellendorf said he had already spent more than $100 since Tuesday to keep his generator running, adding that a tank of fuel typically lasts about 10 hours.

Munster officials said power was restored in some parts of town, but crews were working long hours to fix remaining outages, and urged residents to make way for utility and emergency crews.

“We know this is a stressful time, and we're grateful for your patience and cooperation,” town officials said in a statement. “A little space goes a long way in helping our crews get Munster back up and running safely.”

articles.title: World Vision rapidly assessing emergency needs following powerful Colombia earthquake
articles.description: Country: Colombia Source: World Vision Death toll continues to rise, with more than 180 people confirmed dead and 1,300 injured, as search efforts for missing people remain underway World Vision reports that children amongst most vulnerable Communications and access to the hardest-hit areas remain challenging World Vision is identifying urgent needs, with support focused on shelter, safe water, hygiene, and essential items for children and families World Vision are carrying out rapid emergency assessments following the powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck Colombia on 10 August. World Vison is working with local authorities and organisations to assess needs, identify humanitarian access routes, and determine where assistance is most urgently required. The child-focused humanitarian organisation warns that children are most at risk following the deadly earthquake, which was felt across several major cities, including Bogotá, Manizales, Pereira and Cali, with its epicentre located in the department of Chocó. "Children are particularly vulnerable when emergencies disrupt homes, essential services, and the systems that normally protect them," says Peter Gape, Bi-national Director for Colombia and Venezuela. "Ensuring their safety and wellbeing will remain central to our response. Our teams are working directly with communities, authorities and humanitarian partners to understand where the greatest needs are and how assistance can reach families safely and quickly." World Vision is focusing on the immediate needs of children and families. Planned assistance includes emergency shelter and essential household items such as tarpaulins, tools, blankets, sleeping mats, mosquito nets, kitchen utensils and lamps, along with water filters, hygiene kits, purification tablets and community water storage solutions to address water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) needs. World Vision also plans to establish Child-Friendly Spaces to provide safe environments and activities for children and adolescents affected by the emergency, alongside ready-to-eat food for the most vulnerable. The full impact of the earthquake is still unfolding, with several areas remaining without electricity and water, and communication systems are disrupted and overwhelmed. The earthquake, which had a depth of 88 kilometres, was felt as far as Ecuador and Panama, where metro service was suspended as a precaution following the seismic alert. As the scale of the disaster becomes clearer, attention is turning to the immediate needs of children and families affected. World Vision New Zealand National Director, TJ Grant, says, "New Zealanders know too well how suddenly an earthquake can turn lives upside down. Our teams are already on the ground, working with local partners to understand where the needs are greatest and help ensure children and families get the support they urgently need." articles.title: WHO joins Pakistan and partners to strengthen long-term preparedness for climate-driven floods and stands ready to assist 1.8 million people this year
articles.description: Country: Pakistan Source: World Health Organization Please refer to the attached file. Original publication on WHO Pakistan website. As the health sector stands ready to activate the Monsoon and Flood Contingency Plan 2026 to assist 1.8 million people in high-risk areas, the World Health Organization (WHO) joined the Government of Pakistan, provincial authorities and partners in a national conference to strengthen health emergency preparedness and response to climate-driven hazards over the long term. Under the leadership of the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination, the objective of the National Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Conference was to reinforce short- and long-term emergency preparedness, health sector coordination, timely and efficient data sharing for evidence-based decision-making, resource optimization, and the uninterrupted delivery of essential health services during emergencies, particularly for the most vulnerable, regardless of social or economic status.
